text.p: The departure of Poland's high profile finance minister on Tuesday barely ruffled a feather among foreign investors.
Analysts said that if anything the move could be taken as mildly positive for what has become one of the most successful of East Europe's transition economies.

Polish Brady bonds -- the only Bradys to carry an investment grade rating -- were unchanged after the announcement that Grzegorz Kolodko was quitting to be be replaced as finance minister by Marek Belka.
Polish domestic financial markets were also unworried by the change.
"There's no interest. Noone really cares because Kolodko's successor will persue the same policies," one emerging debt market trader said.
"We wouldn't see this as having an impact on the economic outlook for Poland," said J.P. Morgan analyst Mark Thirlwell.
After the announcement, Belka offered soothing words for investors by pledging to stick to economic policy, including work on pulling down inflation and controlling the budget deficit.
"In some ways it could be a good move. With elections coming up, you need someone less abrasive," one analyst said.
Parliamentary elections are due this autumn.

The analyst said it was vital for Belka, previously economic advisor to the president, to ensure that the macro-economic policy mix had the right balance and that fiscal policy was not too expansionary.
"He's good. He's very clever, very sharp and quite a fun person," West Merchant Bank economist Lina Takla said of Belka, with whom she has worked at the World Bank.
She described him as very much a micro-economist with a strong background in restructuring and knowledge of how to build up small and medium-sized enterprises.
Belka said he would like to see structural reforms speeded up, paying special attention to bank privatisation and reform of social secutiry.
Analysts also expected him to be keen to ensure independence at the central bank which should make for smoother policy on interest rates.
